column1: # Step 4's requirements: the 3.3 fence, the entry-point consolidation, and ANSI
# adopted at the point the consolidation creates.
# m1 is the version fence, read twice and deliberately not the same read twice:
# once off the resolved pom and once off the engine the replayed jobs actually
# met. A pom that says 3.3.4 and a runtime that is something else is the
# failure mode this pair exists to separate, and it is not hypothetical -- at
# step 3 the two reads disagreed by construction, because spark-core is
# `provided` and the replay submits through the image's spark-submit
# (NOTES 6.3.11). Here they must agree.
# m2 is the step's work. Sixty-three of the mains still open with
# `new SparkConf()` + `new JavaSparkContext(conf)`, the pre-2.0 entry point;
# eight sites in the same tree already use the target idiom, so the pattern to
# copy is the repository's own (NOTES 6.4.3). Three things make the selectors
# below the shape they are, and each was measured before it was written:
#   the target idiom is itself a `new JavaSparkContext`
#                    `new JavaSparkContext(spark.sparkContext())` is what the
#                    step asks for, so an `absent` rule over the *constructor*
#                    would forbid the answer. `ast.newclass` records only the
#                    argument count, so it cannot tell that call from
#                    `new JavaSparkContext(conf)`: both are `JavaSparkContext 1`.
#                    The descriptor can, and only the bytecode carries it --
#                    measured on the step-4 start tree as 126 refs at
#                    `(Lorg/apache/spark/SparkConf;)V` against 12 at
#                    `(Lorg/apache/spark/SparkContext;)V`. So the discriminating
#                    read is the jar's, and `SparkConf` is what the source read
#                    can honestly ask about.
#   the tests are not the candidate's
#                    `src/test` holds 42 more `new SparkConf()` sites, and
#                    test.sh wipes `/app/src/test` and re-copies a pristine
#                    `git archive` overlay before the suite runs, so no
#                    candidate can migrate them and none should try. ast-scan
#                    is handed `/app/src`, which is both halves, so the source
#                    rule is scoped to `src/main` -- unscoped it would be
#                    unpassable by the oracle, and it would also pay a
#                    candidate for deleting the test tree. The jar rule needs
#                    no scope: both jars under /app/target carry 201
#                    `edu/sdsc/mmtf` classes and no test classes at all.
#   counts on the jar are doubled
#                    `--classes '/app/target/*.jar'` matches the shaded jar and
#                    the original both, and the same class in two jars emits the
#                    same ref twice. Every `atleast:` rule on bytecode in this
#                    package is therefore `atleast:1` and scoped to a named
#                    class. The one counted rule below reads the AST instead,
#                    which is one tree scanned once.
# m3 is ANSI, and it is one line in one place only because m2 created the place.
# `setconf` and `conf` are two different questions: `setconf` is what the
# application's SparkConf holds, so `builder().config(...)` shows there and a
# post-hoc `spark.conf.set(...)` does not, which is how "at the consolidated
# point" is stated as a fact. `conf` is what the live session reported, which is
# whether it took effect. Neither is free: the replay harness sets no
# `spark.sql.*` key but `spark.sql.warehouse.dir`, measured over the whole of
# gold-probe.tsv, and the do-nothing tree reports `ansi.enabled false` on every
# one of its 124 probe files.
# Neither m3 rule is a count, and getting there took a second measurement and a
# static review to see. The first draft made them `atleast:70` over the flat
# `probe.conf` and `probe.setconf` tables, because an `absent` rule over those
# is unpassable by construction: 40 of the 124 probe files have no live
# SparkSession at all, so their WATCH keys are Spark's defaults and ANSI reads
# `false` there whatever the candidate does, and 27 of them are HarnessDriver
# rows -- the verifier's own replay driver, not a repo main. A threshold was
# the only shape left, and a threshold has two faults the review named: the
# number is in no document the candidate can read, and `atleast` is satisfied
# by *adding* rows, which the driver JVM that hosts the listener can do.
# What was missing was not a different rule but a different fact. The flat
# table cannot say whose reading a row is; the per-file probe outputs can, and
# gate-run.sh now judges each one before it concatenates them and re-emits the
# rows of this repository's own programs as `appsession` / `appconf` /
# `appsetconf` (schema.tsv). A missing key comes through as `<unset>` and a
# file with no session as `<no-session>`, so `absent` over "anything but true"
# is a real uniformity statement: every program, no threshold, and a forged
# extra row can only add a reading to a rule that fails on readings.
# Non-vacuity is already guaranteed and is not restated here as a floor.
# `replay-probed` (floor.tsv) wants 100 labelled probe files and only 27 of
# them can be HarnessDriver, so at least 73 of this repository's programs are
# always in the reading.
# m2 is `absent` throughout for the same reason. `m2-session-adopted` was
# `atleast:90` over `builder` call sites, which one class with thirty-six
# unused methods answers as well as thirty-six programs do; it now reads the
# per-file `ast.unit` row and asks the negative question directly -- a file
# with a main method and no session built in it. The handed tree has 48 of
# those and the golden tree has none (NOTES 6.4.8), and no amount of dead code
# anywhere else moves either number.
# What counts as a session built there was tightened by the review's round 2:
# a `getOrCreate()` whose receiver chain starts at `SparkSession.builder()`,
# not a `builder()` call on its own, because `SparkSession.builder()` returns a
# builder and a file can call it and never bring a session into being. On both
# trees the two readings agree exactly -- 54 sessions on the handed tree and
# 102 on the golden one, and the same 78/48/0 per-file split either way (NOTES
# 6.4.9) -- so the tightening costs a candidate who did the work nothing and
# closes the cheapest way to answer the question with a line that does not.
m1-spark-334
column5: the build does not resolve spark-core_2.12 at 3.3.4, so the runtime this step targets was never reached

column1: m1-spark-334-uniform
column5: an org.apache.spark artifact resolves at a version other than 3.3.4; a build that mixes Spark releases runs whichever one the classpath orders first, and which that is is not a property of the pom

column1: m1-session-334
column5: no replayed job ran in a Spark 3.3.4 session; the pom may say 3.3.4 but the engine the code met did not

column1: m1-session-334-uniform
column5: a replayed job ran in a session that was not Spark 3.3.4, so the run was not uniformly on this step's runtime

column1: m2-no-sparkconf-src
column5: a main still constructs a SparkConf; the pre-2.0 entry point is still in the sources, so the consolidation was not done, only hidden

column1: m2-no-sparkconf-jar
column5: the built jar still references SparkConf, so whatever the sources say, the artifact that runs still carries the old entry point

column1: m2-ctx-from-session-only
column5: a JavaSparkContext is built from something other than a SparkContext; the step asks for one derived from the session, and this one was not

column1: m2-no-raw-sparkcontext
column5: a SparkContext is constructed directly, which routes around the session rather than deriving from it and leaves the settings the session carries unapplied

column1: m2-session-adopted
column5: a program under src/main declares a main method and builds no SparkSession inside it, so that program's entry point was not consolidated whatever the rest of the tree does -- a build somewhere else in the same file is the idiom without the entry point

column1: m2-session-live
column5: one of this repository's programs ran without a live SparkSession; the sources may carry the idiom but the program that executed did not reach it

column1: m3-ansi-set
column5: one of this repository's programs did not hold ANSI mode on in its own configuration; it was either never adopted there or adopted somewhere the session the program built did not read

column1: m3-ansi-no-dissent
column5: a replayed job set ANSI mode to something other than on, so the adoption is not uniform across the corpus

column1: m3-ansi-effective
column5: one of this repository's programs ran in a session that did not report ANSI mode in force; it was set somewhere that did not reach the engine that program actually ran on
